description: Zero-trust secret rotation service that continuously audits credential exposure across repos, cloud configs, and CI pipelines and auto-rotates on detection
opening_quip: Superintendent Chalmers, I present Team VaultKeeper's submission with measured optimism — the problem they have chosen is important, the intent is laudable, and the implementation is, in the most charitable reading, a work in progress that chose the right direction.

dimensions.name: Architecture
dimensions.subtitle: Code structure, layering, and separation of concerns
dimensions.evidence: scanner/, rotator/, auditor/, and api/ packages are logically separated. The rotator calls the scanner directly rather than through an interface, which creates a coupling that would make isolated testing difficult. Service entry points are clean; HTTP and gRPC servers are separate.
dimensions.quip: The package separation is correct in spirit if not entirely in execution — the direct coupling between scanner and rotator is the kind of structural shortcut that feels like a small sin until someone needs to add a second scanner, at which point it becomes a reckoning.

dimensions.name: Integrations
dimensions.subtitle: External systems wired together and called at runtime
dimensions.evidence: GitHub API (repo scanning, secret scanning alerts), AWS Secrets Manager (rotation target), Vault (read/write), and Slack webhook for notifications. GitHub App auth is correct. AWS credentials from instance profile. Vault token renewal not implemented — long-lived token used.
dimensions.quip: Four integrations running at demo time is respectable; the long-lived Vault token is the kind of detail that separates a hackathon project from a production service, and I mention it not to punish but to educate, which is, after all, my vocation.

dimensions.name: Problem Difficulty
dimensions.subtitle: Inherent hardness of the core problem attempted
dimensions.evidence: Secret exposure detection across heterogeneous sources (git history, live config, CI env vars), cross-referencing with cloud IAM to determine blast radius, and triggering provider-specific rotation flows. Each rotation target has a different API shape; the abstraction handles three providers.
dimensions.quip: A blast-radius calculator that queries IAM to determine who can use an exposed credential is the sort of feature that sounds obvious in retrospect and is non-trivial to build, which I appreciate in the same way I appreciate a student who answers the question I asked rather than the one they prepared for.

dimensions.name: Scope Delivered
dimensions.subtitle: How much works end-to-end in the hackathon window
dimensions.evidence: GitHub scanning and Slack alerting are complete and demonstrated. AWS Secrets Manager rotation works for one credential type (RDS passwords). Vault rotation is stubbed with a TODO. GCP Secret Manager listed in the README as supported but not implemented.
dimensions.quip: Two of four advertised features working end-to-end is a B-minus scope by the standards of this rubric, and I award it without rancour — it is an honest B-minus, which is more than I can say for certain other submissions I have scored over the years.

dimensions.name: Engineering Rigor
dimensions.subtitle: Test coverage, CI pipeline, error handling, code quality
dimensions.evidence: 22 test files, mostly unit tests for the scanner regex patterns. No integration tests. CI runs go vet and go test but not a linter. Error handling uses fmt.Errorf consistently but does not wrap errors for stack traces. No structured logging.
dimensions.quip: Twenty-two tests for a security tool that touches live credentials is the number I would describe as 'a beginning' — I mean this gently, as a man who once submitted a gradebook with no validation and learned a great deal from the experience.

dimensions.name: Innovation
dimensions.subtitle: Novelty and creativity of the approach or solution
dimensions.evidence: The blast-radius calculator uses a graph traversal over IAM role assumptions to find all principals that can reach an exposed secret — not just direct holders. The GitHub scanner runs on push webhooks in addition to scheduled full scans to catch secrets before they age.
dimensions.quip: IAM graph traversal for blast-radius attribution is a genuinely clever idea that I had not seen applied to secret scanning before, and I award the point for it with something approaching genuine enthusiasm.

dimensions.name: Operational Readiness
dimensions.subtitle: Containerization, deployment, observability, and reproducibility
dimensions.evidence: Multi-stage Dockerfile, docker-compose.yml with localstack for AWS simulation and a dev Vault. make demo provisions a test secret, exposes it in a dummy repo, and triggers the full detection-rotation loop. No Kubernetes manifests. Logging is unstructured.
dimensions.quip: A Compose stack with LocalStack is a thoughtful developer experience choice — the absence of structured logging in a security audit tool is the one detail I would press on, because an auditor who cannot query their own logs is, as they say in the profession, flying blind.

closing_quip: Forty-six out of seventy. Grade: C. The problem is important and the best ideas here — blast-radius attribution via IAM graph traversal, webhook-triggered scanning — are genuinely worth pursuing. The scope gap and thin test coverage for a security tool are the things I would address before showing this to anyone in a compliance role. I am recommending it as a project to continue, which is the most useful thing I can say about a C.
